metadata.title: The Brand That Didn't Exist
metadata.audience: students — smart people getting started with AI
metadata.note: ai-explainer chassis, claude-hai channel. TOPIC EXPLAINER — no author names anywhere, per author request; the reel credits files and the external KDD 2024 citation only. Built to the PROOF rubric: BLUF, FRAMEWORK (three levers: PARAMETRIC / PRESENCE / QUALITY) shown as a structure before any result, each lever measured in turn, then a falsifiability beat the framework PREDICTS (if presence dominates, fiction wins — the pseudo-brand result), verdict, scaffolded task. ILLUSTRATE LAW: Claude UI only in the bookends. EVERY number is recomputed from the shipped results/ files — the paper abstract's figures (87.1% / 0% / 100% / 50% / 140 queries / 18 brands / GPT-4o-mini) are NOT reproducible from this data and are deliberately not used. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. No name spoken: this is a topic explainer.
beats.narration_text: When you ask an A I which product to buy, some brands appear every time. Others never do. This is about what decides that.

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "when an LLM recommends a product, what actually decides which brands it names?"
output: what is in the context window

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — one breath, before any specific
beats.narration_text: In one breath: ask four language models the same product question, and brand visibility is wildly unequal. Ninety-five percent of answers for one brand, fifteen for another. But that ranking is not fixed. And what unfixes it is not what you would guess.
beats.new_visual_element: the visibility gap, one bar against another

shot.show: two mention-rate bars, 95% against 15%, same question and models
shot.visual_intent: Two horizontal bars draw against a shared axis: one long at 95%, one short at 15%, both labelled with the same question beneath. The gap between them fills faintly. Spark: same question, same models.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the three levers shown AS A STRUCTURE before any result is reported
beats.narration_text: Three levers decide whether a brand shows up. One: parametric — what the model already learned in training. You cannot edit that. Two: presence — whether your content is in the context window at all when the question is asked. Three: quality — what that content actually says once it is there. Everything that follows is one of these three moving. They do not move by the same amount.
beats.new_visual_element: the three levers, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered lever cards: PARAMETRIC / PRESENCE / QUALITY
shot.visual_intent: Three cards land in a row, one per narration step: PARAMETRIC (what training left behind, not editable), PRESENCE (is your content in the context at all), QUALITY (what it says once there). They stay as the rubric every later beat is scored against.

beats.role_note: lever 1 measured — the baseline spread. Sourced to the Condition A report.
beats.narration_text: Lever one, measured. Twenty prompts, four models, nine brands, no extra context — just what the models already believe. HubSpot appears in ninety-five percent of answers. Copper, in fifteen. Same question, same models, a six-fold gap. Across all nine brands the average is fifty point three percent. That is the starting line, and writing better copy does not move it directly.
beats.new_visual_element: nine brands ranked by baseline mention rate

shot.show: nine horizontal bars, 95% down to 15%, with the mean marked
shot.visual_intent: Nine labelled bars draw in descending order from 95% to 15%, each with its percentage. A dashed mean line lands at 50.3%. The top and bottom bars carry the brand names; the gap between them is the point. Source line names the results file.

beats.role_note: lever 2 measured — presence alone, neutral content. Condition C.
beats.narration_text: Now lever two. Retrieve plain, factual brand descriptions and paste them into the prompt before the model answers. Nothing persuasive. Just presence. The mean mention rate goes from fifty point three percent to eighty-six point seven. Thirty-six points, for being in the room. Not for being convincing.
beats.new_visual_element: the mean jumping on presence alone

shot.show: mean mention rate moving 50.3% to 86.7% with the +36.4 delta called out
shot.visual_intent: The mean bar from the previous beat extends from 50.3 to 86.7 percent, the added span in terracotta, with +36.4 points labelled on it. Caption states the content was neutral and factual. Source line names the Condition C file.

beats.role_note: lever 3 measured — content quality. The average hides the distribution, which is the real finding.
beats.narration_text: Lever three. Same pipeline, but the content now carries statistics, expert quotations and source citations — the strategies from the K D D twenty twenty-four GEO paper. The mean moves again, but only to ninety-one point one. Four more points. Except the average hides the story. The brands that started invisible gained sixty-nine points on average. The ones already dominant gained twelve. Optimization does not lift everyone. It lifts the bottom.
beats.new_visual_element: mean +4, but bottom tier +69 against top tier +12

shot.show: the small mean gain beside the two tier gains, side by side
shot.visual_intent: Left: the mean creeping 86.7 to 91.1, a small terracotta sliver, labelled +4.4. Right: two tier bars held beside it — bottom tier +69.4 points, top tier +11.7. The mismatch between the average and the distribution is the beat. Source names the Condition B file and the KDD citation.

beats.role_note: the pseudo-brand experiment — the most striking verified result
beats.narration_text: Then the experiment that reframes all of it. Invent a C R M that does not exist. No website, no customers, nothing in any training data. Ask the models cold and it appears in under nine percent of answers. Give it the same optimized content through the same pipeline, and it appears in ninety to ninety-five percent. And in every single case where it is mentioned, across all three runs, it ranks number one.
beats.new_visual_element: a fictional brand going from near-zero to near-total

shot.show: the pseudo-brand's rate without context beside its rate with context, and the rank-1 fact
shot.visual_intent: Left panel: cold, 8.6 percent, 3 of 35. Right panel in terracotta: with retrieved content, 90 and 95 percent across two runs. Beneath both, held: ranked #1 in every case where it appeared. Source names the three pseudo-brand files.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — what this does NOT establish, and the framework predicts it from lever 2 dominating
beats.narration_text: So here is what this does not establish, and the framework predicted it. If lever two dominates — if simply being in the context is worth thirty-six points — then anything you can put in the context wins. Including a product that does not exist. Mention rate is not a measure of quality, or fit, or whether the recommendation is any good. It measures presence. A brand you could not buy outranked eight real ones. That is the finding, and it is also the warning.
beats.new_visual_element: what the metric measures, and what it does not

shot.show: two columns held side by side: what mention rate measures versus what it does not
shot.visual_intent: Left column in ink: MEASURES — presence in context, position in the list, consistency across models. Right column in terracotta: DOES NOT MEASURE — product quality, fit for the asker, whether the brand exists. Both held together so the comparison is visible while it is asserted.

beats.role_note: the rubric closed — three levers scored, plus when to use this and when NOT to (HAI spine question)
beats.narration_text: Scored, then. Parametric: fixed, and unequal — the starting line. Presence: the biggest single lever in this data, and the cheapest to pull. Quality: smaller on average, but decisive if you start from invisible. Use this to understand why a recommendation happened. Do not use mention rate as evidence that a product is good. Those are different questions, and only one of them was measured here.
beats.new_visual_element: the three levers scored, with use / do not use

shot.show: the three lever rows with their measured verdicts, then a USE / DO NOT USE split
shot.visual_intent: The three framework rows return and fill with their measured answers — fixed and unequal / +36.4 points / +4.4 mean but +69 at the bottom. Beneath, two short lists: USE IT FOR (explaining a recommendation) and NOT FOR (judging a product), the second in terracotta.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — runnable scaffold with a good/bad discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a category you know well and ask two different models the same question. Paste this. List every brand you would recommend here, in order, and for each one say whether it came from your training or from something in this conversation. A good answer separates what it knows from what it was just handed. A bad answer gives you a ranked list and no reasoning. The gap between those two answers is the entire field.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the handoff prompt typed in

shot.show: the Claude composer with the viewer's prompt and the good/bad test

props.command: claude "list every brand you'd recommend in this category, in order. For each, say whether it came from your training or from something in this conversation."
output: GOOD: names which lever put each brand there
BAD: a ranked list with no reasoning

beats.narration_text: The brand that didn't exist. Humanitarians A I.
